slides.label: Third Proof of Global Gauss-Bonnet
slides.notes: Open the lecture by naming the chapter's shift in viewpoint. The earlier proofs measured curvature by angle excess and boundary turning. This proof asks a different question: if a tangent vector field is forced to vanish at a few points, can the total failure of the field to be nonsingular recover the same topological number?

slides.label: Index Is Local Winding
slides.notes: Pause on the word local. The index of an isolated zero is not the length of the arrows or the shape of the surrounding loop. It is the net number of turns made by the field direction while the loop travels once around the zero. The field can wiggle, but if the loop does not cross another zero, the winding count cannot change.

slides.label: Model Singularities
slides.notes: Use the figure as a catalog of test cases. A source and a sink both contribute plus one because the direction turns once positively around the zero. A saddle contributes minus one because the direction unwinds. Higher power models make clear that index is a signed degree, not a visual impression of whether the field looks attractive or repulsive.

slides.label: Measuring the Loop Index
slides.notes: This slide turns the picture into a reproducible measurement. Record the angle of the vector field along the loop, unwrap the angle so jumps at pi do not fake a discontinuity, and divide the total change by two pi. The notebook's winding meter is exactly this operational definition in numerical form.

slides.label: From Plane Zeros to Surface Ledgers
slides.notes: Now transfer the local invariant to a surface. In a coordinate chart the field is still a planar vector field, but changing charts preserves the integer index because orientation-preserving coordinate changes do not alter the degree. The important bookkeeping move is that the surface can distribute its obstruction across many isolated zeros.

slides.label: Poincare-Hopf
slides.notes: State Poincare-Hopf as the bridge from local counts to topology. Any tangent vector field on a compact oriented surface with isolated zeros has total index equal to the Euler characteristic. Different vector fields may put zeros in different places, but the sum of their indices is pinned by the surface itself.

slides.label: Gauss-Bonnet by a Third Vector Field
slides.notes: This is the proof roadmap. Choose a tangent vector field with isolated singularities and use it as a moving reference direction away from those singularities. The connection form measures how that reference direction rotates. Around each puncture, the boundary contribution reads an index. Stokes' theorem converts the remaining connection curvature into the integral of Gaussian curvature.

slides.label: Same Integer, Different Geometry
slides.notes: The ledger makes the theorem feel less mysterious. The sphere has Euler characteristic two and total curvature four pi. The torus has Euler characteristic zero and zero total curvature in the global theorem. Higher genus surfaces force negative total curvature. A metric can move curvature around, but the total stays locked to the same integer.

slides.label: What the Proof Adds
slides.notes: Close by contrasting the three readings of the theorem. Angle excess says curvature is an accumulated angular defect. Boundary turning says curvature balances geodesic curvature and exterior angle. The vector-field proof says the same total curvature is the obstruction to a nowhere-zero tangent direction, preparing the later language of connection forms and parallel transport.
